```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::knit_hooks$set(small_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(small_mar = TRUE)

occ <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")

occ_nll <- function(p){
  prob <- plogis(p[1] + p[2] * occ$elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
}

# brute force
a_vec <- seq(1, 3, by = 0.01)
b_vec <- seq(-0.15, 0.05, by = 0.001)
grid <- expand.grid(a = a_vec, b = b_vec)
t_grid <- system.time({
  grid$nll <- NA
  for (i in 1:nrow(grid)) {
    grid$nll[i] <- occ_nll(c(grid$a[i], grid$b[i]))
  }
})[["elapsed"]]
best_grid <- grid[which.min(grid$nll), ]
per_eval <- t_grid / nrow(grid)

fit_nm   <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll)
fit_bfgs <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll, method = "BFGS")
fit_cg   <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll, method = "CG")
set.seed(1)
fit_sa1  <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll, method = "SANN")
set.seed(2026)
fit_sa2  <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll, method = "SANN")
t_opt <- system.time(for (r in 1:100) optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll))[["elapsed"]] / 100

# record every point each method tries, for the path figure
trace_fit <- function(method, seed = NULL){
  pts <- list()
  f <- function(p){
    pts[[length(pts) + 1]] <<- p
    occ_nll(p)
  }
  if (!is.null(seed)) { set.seed(seed) }
  optim(c(0, 0), f, method = method)
  do.call(rbind, pts)
}
path_nm   <- trace_fit("Nelder-Mead")
path_bfgs <- trace_fit("BFGS")
path_sa   <- trace_fit("SANN", seed = 1)

# the reef hump: multi-start, the profile over width, and the plateau
reef <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/reef_surveys.csv")
reef_nll <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1]) * exp(-(reef$depth - p[2])^2 / (2 * exp(p[3])^2))
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = mu, size = exp(p[4]), log = TRUE))
}
reef_start <- function(){
  c(log(runif(1, 5, 50)), runif(1, 0, 30), log(runif(1, 1, 50)), log(runif(1, 1, 20)))
}
set.seed(19)
reef_ms <- NULL
for (i in 1:10) {
  fit <- optim(reef_start(), reef_nll)
  reef_ms <- rbind(reef_ms, c(peak = exp(fit$par[1]), depth = fit$par[2],
                              width = exp(fit$par[3]), nll = fit$value,
                              convergence = fit$convergence))
}
reef_best <- optim(c(log(20), 15, log(10), log(5)), reef_nll)
reef_hits <- sum(reef_ms[, "nll"] < reef_best$value + 0.1)

# the same ten random starts on the two-parameter occupancy model
set.seed(19)
occ_ends <- replicate(10, optim(c(runif(1, -5, 5), runif(1, -1, 1)), occ_nll)$value)
occ_hits <- sum(occ_ends < fit_bfgs$value + 0.01)

# profile over width, each fit starting from the previous one's answer
reef_widths <- exp(seq(log(8), log(5000), length.out = 16))
reef_prof <- numeric(length(reef_widths))
q <- reef_best$par[-3]
for (k in seq_along(reef_widths)) {
  pf <- optim(q, function(qq){ reef_nll(c(qq[1], qq[2], log(reef_widths[k]), qq[3])) })
  q <- pf$par
  reef_prof[k] <- pf$value - reef_best$value
}
reef_flat <- optim(c(log(23), log(5)), function(q){
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = exp(q[1]), size = exp(q[2]), log = TRUE))
})
reef_flat_gap <- reef_flat$value - reef_best$value
reef_bins <- cut(reef$depth, breaks = seq(0, 32, by = 2))
reef_bin_depth <- tapply(reef$depth, reef_bins, mean)
reef_bin_rich <- tapply(reef$richness, reef_bins, mean)

# simulating from the occupancy fit
p_fit <- plogis(fit_bfgs$par[1] + fit_bfgs$par[2] * occ$elapsed)
set.seed(1)
fake <- replicate(1000, rbinom(nrow(occ), size = occ$n_routes, prob = p_fit) / occ$n_routes)
occ_lower <- apply(fake, 1, quantile, 0.025)
occ_upper <- apply(fake, 1, quantile, 0.975)
occ_obs <- occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes
occ_inside <- sum(occ_obs >= occ_lower & occ_obs <= occ_upper)

# the challenge: a threshold in development
counts_ch <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")
threshold_nll <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1] + p[2] * pmax(0, counts_ch$frac_built - p[3]))
  -sum(dnbinom(counts_ch$count, mu = mu, size = exp(p[4]), log = TRUE))
}
ch_first <- optim(c(2, -1, 0.3, 0), threshold_nll)
ch_lbfgsb <- optim(c(2, -1, 0.3, 0), threshold_nll, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 0, -Inf), upper = c(Inf, Inf, 0.48, Inf))
ch_tgrid <- seq(-0.2, 0.7, by = 0.01)
ch_prof <- numeric(length(ch_tgrid))
q <- c(2.5, -3, 0.4)
for (k in seq_along(ch_tgrid)) {
  pf <- optim(q, function(qq){ threshold_nll(c(qq[1], qq[2], ch_tgrid[k], qq[3])) })
  q <- pf$par
  ch_prof[k] <- pf$value
}
t_best <- ch_tgrid[which.min(ch_prof)]
ch_best <- optim(c(2.5, -3.4, t_best, 0.4), threshold_nll)
ch_flat <- optim(c(2.5, 0.4), function(q){
  -sum(dnbinom(counts_ch$count, mu = exp(q[1]), size = exp(q[2]), log = TRUE))
})$value
set.seed(2)
ch_ms <- replicate(20, optim(c(runif(1, 0, 4), runif(1, -10, 0), runif(1, 0, 0.45),
                               runif(1, -1, 2)), threshold_nll)$value)

fmt_time <- function(sec){
  if (sec < 60) { return(paste(signif(sec, 2), "seconds")) }
  if (sec < 3600) { return(paste(round(sec / 60), "minutes")) }
  if (sec < 86400) { return(paste(round(sec / 3600, 1), "hours")) }
  if (sec < 86400 * 365) { return(paste(round(sec / 86400), "days")) }
  paste(round(sec / 86400 / 365, 1), "years")
}
```

## Today's agenda {.smaller}

- R has found the bottom of every NLL curve for us. **How?**
- Trying every value, and why that stops working
- Three ways to walk downhill: **Nelder-Mead, BFGS, simulated annealing**
- How to tell whether a fit **actually worked**, and whether it **fits the data**
- A challenge: who can get the **best fit**?

. . .

[Type and run]{.type-badge} on a code block: type it into your script and run it.
Code without the label is there to watch.

::: {.notes}
Bolker 7.1 and 7.2. Students have called optim() and mle2() a dozen times and
been told they "find the minimum". Today opens the box, for two reasons: the
method argument has been in their code for weeks without explanation, and
Thursday's lecture on what goes wrong (7.4) needs to know how the search works.

Kept short on purpose, after Lecture 18 ran long.
:::

## The story so far {.smaller}

- **Lower NLL = better fit.** The best estimate is the bottom of the curve
- Intervals and model comparisons read the **shape** of that curve
- **Today:** how R finds the bottom in the first place, and how to tell when it
  did not

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The connection worth making: every number since Lecture 15
assumed the optimizer found the true bottom. If it did not, the estimates, the
intervals and the AIC are all wrong together.
:::

## Why does R need an algorithm at all? {.smaller}

Sometimes the bottom has a formula. For 52 routes occupied out of 71, the best
$p$ is just $52 / 71$.

. . .

For the logistic decline,

$$p_t = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(a + bt)}}$$

**there is no formula** for the best $a$ and $b$. The only way to find them is to
**search**: try values, see which give a lower NLL, and try again.

. . .

An optimizer is a **search strategy**. The `method` argument chooses which one.

::: {.notes}
Bolker opens chapter 7 with the same point. Most models worth fitting have no
closed-form answer, so every fit in this course has been a search.

Ask: who has seen method = "BFGS" or method = "L-BFGS-B" in their code without
knowing what it did? Most hands go up. That is today.
:::

## Get set up {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(bbmle)
library(biometrydata)

occ <- bobwhite_occupancy

# the occupancy model, with both parameters in one vector, as optim() wants
occ_nll <- function(p){
  prob <- plogis(p[1] + p[2] * occ$elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
}

occ_nll(c(2, -0.05))    # one guess: how good is it?
```
:::

**Check:** about `r round(occ_nll(c(2, -0.05)), 1)`. The best possible, from
Lecture 16, is `r round(fit_bfgs$value, 2)`.

::: {.notes}
The same model as Lectures 16 to 18, written as a function of one vector p, which
is the form optim() expects: p[1] is a, the log odds of occupancy in 1997, and
p[2] is b, the yearly change.

Calling it by hand once makes the point that an NLL function is just a scoring
rule: give it a guess, it returns how bad the guess is. Every method today is a
different strategy for choosing the next guess.
:::

# Trying every value

## Brute force {.smaller}

The simplest strategy: lay a **grid** over the surface and score every point.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-width: 7.4
z <- matrix(grid$nll, nrow = length(a_vec))
contour(a_vec, b_vec, z, levels = c(57, 58, 60, 65, 75, 100, 150, 250),
        xlab = "a", ylab = "b", col = "grey55", labcex = 0.7)
gs <- expand.grid(a = seq(1, 3, by = 0.1), b = seq(-0.15, 0.05, by = 0.01))
points(gs$a, gs$b, pch = 3, cex = 0.35, col = "#2a7ab0")
points(best_grid$a, best_grid$b, pch = 16, cex = 1.4, col = "red")
```

Blue crosses: a sample of the grid, every tenth point in each direction. The real
one has **`r format(nrow(grid), big.mark = ",")`** points.

::: {.notes}
The red dot is the lowest grid point. Nothing clever is happening: no point is
chosen because of any other.

Two problems are visible already. The answer can only be a grid point, so it is
only as precise as the spacing. And the grid only covers the box someone chose;
if the bottom were outside it, brute force would report the edge of the box
without any warning.
:::

## Your turn: brute force {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
a_vec <- seq(1, 3, by = 0.01)
b_vec <- seq(-0.15, 0.05, by = 0.001)
grid <- expand.grid(a = a_vec, b = b_vec)    # every combination
nrow(grid)

grid_time <- system.time({
  grid$nll <- NA
  for (i in 1:nrow(grid)) {
    grid$nll[i] <- occ_nll(c(grid$a[i], grid$b[i]))
  }
})
grid_time

grid[which.min(grid$nll), ]                  # the best grid point
```
:::

**Check:** best $a$ = `r best_grid$a`, $b$ = `r best_grid$b`, against
`r round(fit_bfgs$par[1], 3)` and `r round(fit_bfgs$par[2], 4)` from `optim()`.

::: {.notes}
Two or three minutes. It takes a few seconds to run, which is part of the
lesson; let them wait.

expand.grid() is the new function: it builds every combination of the values it
is given, one row each. system.time() is the other: elapsed is the number to
read.

The answer matches optim() to the spacing of the grid and no further.
:::

## How slow is slow? {.smaller}

| | Evaluations | Time |
|---|---|---|
| brute force, 2 parameters | `r format(nrow(grid), big.mark = ",")` | `r fmt_time(t_grid)` |
| `optim()`, 2 parameters | `r fit_nm$counts[["function"]]` | `r signif(t_opt * 1000, 2)` thousandths of a second |

. . .

With **100 values per parameter**, brute force needs $100^k$ evaluations:

| Parameters | Evaluations | Time |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 10 thousand | `r fmt_time(1e4 * per_eval)` |
| 4 | 100 million | `r fmt_time(1e8 * per_eval)` |
| **6** | **1 trillion** | **`r fmt_time(1e12 * per_eval)`** |

::: {.plain}
Trying every value works for one or two parameters. Beyond that, it would outlast the semester, and then the degree.
:::

::: {.notes}
The times are from this computer, while rendering these slides, so theirs will
differ a little; the shape will not.

Six parameters is not a big model. The two-species model on Thursday had six.

Brute force is still useful in one way: for one or two parameters, a coarse grid
is a fast way to see the whole surface and pick sensible starting values. Bolker
says the same.
:::

# Walking downhill

## Three strategies {.smaller}

Every method starts at a guess and moves **downhill**. They differ in how they
choose the next step:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 9
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 2, 0.4), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0),
    cex.axis = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.3, cex.main = 1.5)
a2 <- seq(-0.5, 3, length.out = 120)
b2 <- seq(-0.2, 0.12, length.out = 120)
z2 <- outer(a2, b2, Vectorize(function(a, b){ occ_nll(c(a, b)) }))
paths <- list("Nelder-Mead" = path_nm, "BFGS" = path_bfgs,
              "simulated annealing" = path_sa)
for (nm in names(paths)) {
  contour(a2, b2, log(z2), nlevels = 14, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey70",
          xlab = "a", ylab = "b", main = nm)
  pth <- paths[[nm]]
  if (nm == "simulated annealing") {
    points(pth[, 1], pth[, 2], pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
           col = adjustcolor("#762a83", 0.25))
  } else {
    lines(pth[, 1], pth[, 2], col = "#762a83", lwd = 1.5)
    points(pth[, 1], pth[, 2], pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = "#762a83")
  }
  if (nm == "BFGS") {
    text(0.15, 0.1, "first stride:
off the map", pos = 4, cex = 1.2,
         col = "#762a83")
  }
  points(0, 0, pch = 17, cex = 2, col = "#1b7837")
  points(fit_bfgs$par[1], fit_bfgs$par[2], pch = 16, cex = 2, col = "red")
}
```

Green: the start. Red: the bottom. Purple: **every point each method tried**.

::: {.notes}
The one figure to linger on. All three start at a = 0, b = 0 and end at the same
bottom.

Nelder-Mead feels its way down with a small triangle of points. BFGS takes a few
long, confident strides, because it uses the slope; its very first stride, from a
slope measured at a poor start, overshoots to a = 494, b = 4,610, far off the
map, and it backs up from there in shrinking steps. Simulated annealing sprays
points everywhere, including uphill, and only settles down at the end.

The contour lines are drawn on a log scale so the shape of the valley is visible
far from the bottom.
:::

## Nelder-Mead {.smaller}

A **triangle** of three guesses tumbles downhill. Each step, the worst corner is
flipped across the other two; the triangle stretches when that works and shrinks
when it does not.

- Needs **only the NLL itself**, no slopes
- Copes with rough or awkward surfaces
- **`optim()`'s default**

::: {.plain}
Keep the best guesses, replace the worst one, repeat until the guesses stop improving.
:::

::: {.notes}
Bolker 7.2 calls it the simplex method. With two parameters the simplex is a
triangle; with k parameters it has k + 1 corners.

Its weakness is speed on well-behaved problems, where using the slope would get there
in fewer steps, which is the next slide.
:::

## BFGS {.smaller}

Uses the **slope** of the surface, and how the slope is changing, to aim straight
for the bottom.

- **Fast** when the surface is well behaved: fewer evaluations
- Needs a surface with **no corners or cliffs**, and a start that is not absurd
- **`mle2()`'s default**

::: {.plain}
Look at which way is downhill and how steeply, then take a long stride in that direction.
:::

::: {.notes}
Named for Broyden, Fletcher, Goldfarb and Shanno. R does not need a formula for
the slope: it estimates it by nudging each parameter a tiny amount and seeing how
the NLL changes. That is what the second number in counts is.

The important thing to remember is the defaults: optim() uses Nelder-Mead,
mle2() uses BFGS. Students who switch between the two and see slightly different
answers have usually met that difference.
:::

## Your turn: two methods {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_nm   <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll)                    # Nelder-Mead, the default
fit_bfgs <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll, method = "BFGS")

fit_nm$par;   fit_nm$value;   fit_nm$counts
fit_bfgs$par; fit_bfgs$value; fit_bfgs$counts
```
:::

**Same answer? Which needed fewer evaluations?**

. . .

| | $a$ | $b$ | NLL | evaluations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nelder-Mead | `r round(fit_nm$par[1], 4)` | `r round(fit_nm$par[2], 5)` | `r round(fit_nm$value, 3)` | `r fit_nm$counts[["function"]]` |
| BFGS | `r round(fit_bfgs$par[1], 4)` | `r round(fit_bfgs$par[2], 5)` | `r round(fit_bfgs$value, 3)` | `r fit_bfgs$counts[["function"]]` + `r fit_bfgs$counts[["gradient"]]` slopes |

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. The answers agree to three decimals; the differences in the fourth
are each method's stopping rule, not a disagreement about the model.

counts has two numbers: how many times the NLL was computed, and how many times
the slope was. Nelder-Mead never computes a slope, hence NA.

Starting both at (0, 0) on purpose: a deliberately poor start, far from the
answer, and both still find it. This surface is well behaved. Thursday is about
the ones that are not.
:::

## Simulated annealing {.smaller}

Takes **random** steps, and sometimes accepts one that goes **uphill**. Accepts
fewer uphill steps as it "cools".

- Can escape a **false bottom**, a dip that is not the lowest point
- **Slow**: always `r format(fit_sa1$counts[["function"]], big.mark = ",")` evaluations here
- **Random**: a different answer every run, unless you `set.seed()`

::: {.plain}
Wander widely at first so you do not get stuck in the wrong valley, then settle down.
:::

::: {.notes}
Named for annealing metal: heat it so the atoms can move, then cool it slowly so
they settle into a low-energy arrangement. The "temperature" controls how willing
the search is to go uphill.

Its strength is surfaces with several dips, where a downhill-only method stops in
whichever dip it starts near. Our occupancy surface has one bottom, so here it
only shows its costs: slower, and slightly less precise.

method = "SANN" in R. It always runs a fixed number of steps, so its convergence
code is always 0 and tells you nothing.
:::

## Your turn: annealing twice {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1)
fit_sa1 <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll, method = "SANN")

set.seed(2026)
fit_sa2 <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll, method = "SANN")

fit_sa1$par; fit_sa1$value
fit_sa2$par; fit_sa2$value
```
:::

**Do the two runs agree? How close are they to BFGS?**

. . .

Close, not identical: NLLs of `r round(fit_sa1$value, 3)` and
`r round(fit_sa2$value, 3)`, against `r round(fit_bfgs$value, 3)`. A common habit
is to **anneal first, then polish** with BFGS, starting from where annealing
stopped.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Without set.seed() everyone in the room gets a different answer,
which is worth letting them see by comparing with a neighbor first.

Anneal then polish: optim(fit_sa1$par, occ_nll, method = "BFGS") lands on the
exact bottom. Annealing finds the right valley; BFGS finds the bottom of it.
:::

## Two specialists you have already used {.smaller}

| Method | For | Where you met it |
|---|---|---|
| `"L-BFGS-B"` | BFGS with **bounds** on each parameter | Lecture 16, keeping `size` positive |
| `optimize()` | **one** parameter only | Lecture 15, the single-$p$ fits |

. . .

`mle2()` takes the same names: `mle2(..., method = "Nelder-Mead")`.

::: {.notes}
A callback rather than new material. The bounds in Lecture 16 needed L-BFGS-B
because plain BFGS does not accept lower and upper.

optimize() is a different function from optim(), not a method of it, which
trips people up. For one parameter it is the right tool; optim() warns if you
give it a single parameter with Nelder-Mead.
:::

# Did it work?

## A fit can fail without an error {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_cg <- optim(c(0, 0), occ_nll, method = "CG")    # another method optim() offers

fit_cg$par
fit_cg$value
fit_cg$convergence
```
:::

. . .

$a$ = `r round(fit_cg$par[1], 3)`, $b$ = `r round(fit_cg$par[2], 4)`, NLL
**`r round(fit_cg$value, 1)`**, against `r round(fit_bfgs$value, 1)` at the true
bottom. **No error. No warning.**

The only clue: `convergence` is **`r fit_cg$convergence`**, not 0. It ran out of
steps before it got there.

::: {.notes}
The most important slide today. CG, conjugate gradients, is a legitimate method
that is slow on this surface, and with the default step limit it simply stops
partway down the valley and hands back wherever it was.

A b of -0.006 instead of -0.062 is a decline ten times too small, reported with
complete confidence. Everything downstream, intervals and AIC included, would be
wrong.

convergence: 0 means the method believes it reached a bottom. 1 means it hit
the iteration limit. Other numbers are method-specific trouble. mle2() checks it
for you and prints a warning; optim() does not.
:::

# Surfaces that are hard to search

## A false bottom you cannot see from inside {.smaller}

Lecture 16's practice problem: reef fish richness **peaks at some depth**, a hump
with a height, a location and a **width**. The NLL as the width changes, with the
other parameters re-fitted at each width:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-width: 7.4
plot(reef_widths, reef_prof, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#762a83", log = "x",
     xlab = "width of the hump (m, log scale)", ylab = "NLL above the best",
     bty = "l", ylim = c(0, 60))
abline(h = reef_flat_gap, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
text(max(reef_widths), reef_flat_gap + 4, "a flat line: no depth effect at all",
     pos = 2, cex = 0.85, col = "grey35")
points(exp(reef_best$par[3]), 0, pch = 16, cex = 1.6, col = "red")
```

A wide enough hump **is** a flat line. Out there the NLL stops changing, so a
downhill method sees **no slope** and stops, reporting success.

::: {.notes}
Read the curve from left to right. Narrow humps fit terribly (off the top). The
best width is about 24 m, the red dot. Wider than that, the NLL climbs, then
levels off at exactly the NLL of a model with no depth effect, the dashed line,
46.65 units worse. Make the hump thousands of metres wide and it is flat across
every depth in the data, so it simply is the flat model.

That plateau is the trap. A simple bowl has one bottom and every downhill path
leads to it. A plateau has no downhill: an optimizer that wanders onto it sees a
slope of zero in every direction, concludes it has arrived, and returns
convergence = 0. Nothing in the output looks wrong.

Showing the width rather than all four parameters at once is the slices and
profiles idea from Lecture 17: the only way to look at a surface with more than
two parameters.
:::

## What makes a surface hard to search {.smaller}

| The surface has | What goes wrong | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|
| a **plateau**: a parameter stops mattering (the hump's width) | no slope, so it stops and reports success | better starts, bounds, or a simpler model |
| **several dips**: rival explanations fit almost as well | stops in whichever dip is nearest | many starts, or simulated annealing |
| a **ridge**: two parameters that trade off | zigzags slowly along the valley | re-parameterize (Thursday) |
| a **cliff**: an `if` or a penalty in the code | BFGS needs a slope, and there is none at a cliff | Nelder-Mead, or rewrite the model |

::: {.plain}
Each kind of trouble has its own fix, so the first job is to notice which one you have.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four shapes, none exotic. The plateau is today's reef example. Several dips is
what simulated annealing exists for. A ridge is the tilted valley from Lecture
17, stretched out: two parameters that can compensate for each other, so the
data pin down a combination of them but not each one. A cliff comes from code,
not biology: any if() inside an NLL function, or a penalty like the 1e6 that
guarded the straight-line occupancy model in Lecture 16.

On vocabulary, since "smooth" gets used two ways: to an optimizer, a smooth
surface is one with no corners or cliffs, so the slope is defined everywhere.
Plateaus and ridges can be perfectly smooth in that sense and still be hard to
search. That is why the table names shapes rather than saying smooth or rough.

Thursday (Bolker 7.4) goes into each fix. Today is about noticing.
:::

## Check: start from many places {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
reef <- reef_surveys

# p[1] log of the peak richness, p[2] depth of the peak (m),
# p[3] log of the width (m), p[4] log of the negative binomial size
reef_nll <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1]) * exp(-(reef$depth - p[2])^2 / (2 * exp(p[3])^2))
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = mu, size = exp(p[4]), log = TRUE))
}

set.seed(19)
results <- NULL
for (i in 1:10) {
  start <- c(log(runif(1, 5, 50)), runif(1, 0, 30), log(runif(1, 1, 50)), log(runif(1, 1, 20)))
  fit <- optim(start, reef_nll)
  results <- rbind(results, c(peak = exp(fit$par[1]), depth = fit$par[2],
                              width = exp(fit$par[3]), nll = fit$value,
                              convergence = fit$convergence))
}
round(results, 1)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Ten fits from ten random starts. It takes about fifteen seconds; let it run.

The parameters are fitted on the log scale where they must be positive, the
"keeping parameters legal" table from Lecture 16, and exp() turns them back for
the table.

runif() draws each starting value from a sensible range: a peak of 5 to 50
species, a depth of 0 to 30 m, a width of 1 to 50 m. set.seed(19) makes
everyone's starts the same, so the room can compare tables.
:::

## What ten starts found {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(round(reef_ms[order(reef_ms[, "nll"]), ], 1)),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

**`r reef_hits` of 10** reach the best NLL; the rest stop up to
`r round(max(reef_ms[, "nll"]) - min(reef_ms[, "nll"]))` worse. **All** report `convergence = 0`.

::: {.notes}
The top rows agree: a peak of about 25 species at about 16 m, with a width of
about 24 m. The others stopped somewhere else entirely, some with a peak at the
deep end and a very wide hump, sliding toward the plateau.

The point of the exercise: the convergence code was 0 every time. Only running
it more than once revealed that some answers were wrong. With one fit, a student
could have reported any row of this table.

The rule: always run a model with several parameters from several starts, and
report the one with the lowest NLL. If the best few agree, that is reassurance.
:::

## More parameters: harder to search {.smaller}

| Model | Parameters | Random starts that found the best fit |
|---|---|---|
| bobwhite occupancy | 2 | **`r occ_hits` of 10** |
| reef hump | 4 | **`r reef_hits` of 10** |

. . .

Why more parameters make the search harder:

- You **cannot look** at a surface with more than two parameters
- More chances for parameters to **trade off**, making ridges and plateaus
- More room for **false bottoms**, so you need **more starts** to trust an answer

::: {.notes}
More parameters create more opportunities for trouble, not a guarantee of it.
Adding a term to the linear part of a logistic or Poisson regression, for
instance, can never create a second dip: those likelihoods have a single bottom
however many predictors they have. The trouble comes from parameters that can
trade off, or that can make another one irrelevant, as the hump's width does to
its depth, and those become more likely as models grow.

So the practical consequence is the one students need: the more parameters, the
more starts it takes before an answer can be trusted, and the more important the
checks on the next slides become.

The occupancy row is the same exercise, same seed, run on the two-parameter
model. In testing, 30 of 30 starts found its bottom against 11 of 30 for the
reef hump.
:::

# Does the model fit the data?

## Draw the fit over the data {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# richness averaged in 2 m depth bins: 8,560 surveys are too many to read
bins <- cut(reef$depth, breaks = seq(0, 32, by = 2))
plot(tapply(reef$depth, bins, mean), tapply(reef$richness, bins, mean),
     pch = 16, xlab = "depth (m)", ylab = "mean species richness")

hump <- function(d, row){
  results[row, "peak"] * exp(-(d - results[row, "depth"])^2 / (2 * results[row, "width"]^2))
}
best <- which.min(results[, "nll"])
worst <- which.max(results[, "nll"])
curve(hump(x, best), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 3)
curve(hump(x, worst), add = TRUE, col = "grey50", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| fig-width: 7
plot(reef_bin_depth, reef_bin_rich, pch = 16, xlab = "depth (m)",
     ylab = "mean richness", bty = "l")
hump_draw <- function(d, row){
  reef_ms[row, "peak"] * exp(-(d - reef_ms[row, "depth"])^2 / (2 * reef_ms[row, "width"]^2))
}
curve(hump_draw(x, which.min(reef_ms[, "nll"])), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 3)
curve(hump_draw(x, which.max(reef_ms[, "nll"])), add = TRUE, col = "grey50",
      lwd = 3, lty = 2)
```

::: {.notes}
The plot that catches what the convergence code missed. The red curve, the best
fit, follows the binned means up and over the hump. The dashed curve, the worst
of the ten, misses the shape of the data: a failed fit is usually obvious the
moment it is drawn.

Binned means are a check, not part of the fit: 8,560 points would be a solid
smear, and averaging within depth bins shows the trend the model is trying to
capture.
:::

## Simulate from the fit {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**If the model were true, would it produce data like ours?**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_occ <- optim(c(2, -0.05), occ_nll, method = "BFGS")
p_fit <- plogis(fit_occ$par[1] + fit_occ$par[2] * occ$elapsed)

# 1,000 imaginary sets of surveys, from the fitted model
fake <- replicate(1000, rbinom(nrow(occ), size = occ$n_routes, prob = p_fit) / occ$n_routes)
lower <- apply(fake, 1, quantile, 0.025)    # the middle 95% of the fakes,
upper <- apply(fake, 1, quantile, 0.975)    # year by year

plot(occ$year, occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes, pch = 16, ylim = c(0.5, 1),
     xlab = "year", ylab = "fraction of routes occupied")
lines(occ$year, lower, lty = 2)
lines(occ$year, upper, lty = 2)
```
:::

**Check:** `r occ_inside` of `r nrow(occ)` real years fall inside the band.

::: {.notes}
Lecture 13's simulation idea, pointed at a fitted model. Each fake dataset is
what the fitted logistic curve plus binomial scatter would produce. If the real
points sat outside the band, the model would be missing something: a trend it
does not have, or more scatter than the binomial allows.

Here all of them sit inside: the model reproduces the data it was fitted to,
which is what a good fit should do. About 1 point in 20 outside would also be
fine; most outside would not.

This is the same check as comparing a histogram of real counts with simulated
ones, the way the negative binomial earned its place against the Poisson. It
works for any model that can be simulated from, which is every model in this
course.
:::

## Checking a fit {.smaller}

1. **`convergence` is 0.** With `mle2()`, no warning about convergence
2. **Several starts agree.** Report the lowest NLL; more parameters, more starts
3. **The fitted curve goes through the data.** Draw it
4. **Data simulated from the fit look like the real data**
5. **A bigger model never fits worse than a smaller one nested in it.** If it
   does, it has not found its bottom

::: {.plain}
Never trust a fit just because R returned numbers. Check that it stopped for the right reason, and that it agrees with itself.
:::

::: {.notes}
A checklist for Assignment 3. Item 4 is the one students do not think of: a
bigger model can never fit worse than a model nested inside it (Lecture 18), so
if it does, the optimizer stopped early.

Thursday, 7.4, is the catalogue of why fits fail: bad starting values,
parameters on wildly different scales, flat or bumpy surfaces. This checklist is
how they will notice.
:::

## Which method, when {.smaller}

| Method | Use it when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| brute force | 1 or 2 parameters, or to find a starting point | impossibly slow beyond that |
| Nelder-Mead | the default; awkward surfaces | slower than BFGS |
| BFGS | no corners or cliffs; `mle2()`'s default | can fail from a bad start |
| L-BFGS-B | parameters need bounds | |
| simulated annealing | several dips; nothing else works | slow, random: `set.seed()` |

**Whatever you use: check `convergence`.**

::: {.notes}
The summary slide. The practical advice for the assignment: start with the
default, and if it fails or the convergence code is not 0, try a second method
from the same start.
:::

# Challenge

## Challenge: who can get the lowest NLL? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**Does development hurt bobwhite only past a threshold?** Counts stay flat until a
route is $t$ developed, then fall:

$$\mu = \mu_0 \, e^{\,b \cdot \max(0,\; u - t)} \qquad \text{count} \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu, k)$$

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
counts <- bobwhite_counts

# p[1] log mu0, p[2] slope b, p[3] threshold t (fraction developed), p[4] log k
threshold_nll <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1] + p[2] * pmax(0, counts$frac_built - p[3]))
  -sum(dnbinom(counts$count, mu = mu, size = exp(p[4]), log = TRUE))
}

start <- c(2, -1, 0.3, 0)
first_try <- optim(start, threshold_nll)
first_try$value
```
:::

**Beat it.** Any method, any start, any trick from today. Write down your lowest
NLL, and **how** you got it.

::: {.notes}
Fifteen minutes, in pairs if the room prefers. The first try gives about
`r round(ch_first$value, 2)`; the best possible is about
`r round(ch_best$value, 2)`. Put the first try on the board and keep a running
best, with names and methods, as people improve on it.

pmax(0, u - t) is the new piece: it is zero for any route less than t developed,
so those routes all get the same expected count, mu0. Above t, counts fall
exponentially, as in Lecture 16's development model.

Hints, in order, for anyone stuck after five minutes:

1. Look at first_try$par. Is the threshold a sensible fraction developed? The
   routes run from 0 to about 0.49.
2. Today's table of hard surfaces. What kind of trouble is a threshold that
   wanders outside the data?
3. Brute force works well for a single parameter.

Do not reveal the next slide until the board has settled.
:::

## How the room could have won {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| fig-width: 7.6
plot(ch_tgrid, ch_prof - ch_best$value, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#762a83",
     xlab = "threshold t (fraction developed)", ylab = "NLL above the best",
     bty = "l")
abline(v = range(counts_ch$frac_built), lty = 3, col = "grey50")
text(-0.08, ch_first$value - ch_best$value + 4, "no threshold", cex = 0.8, col = "grey35")
text(0.6, ch_flat - ch_best$value - 6, "no development effect", cex = 0.8, col = "grey35")
points(ch_best$par[3], 0, pch = 16, cex = 1.6, col = "red")
text(ch_best$par[3], 8, "best", cex = 0.8, col = "red")
```

| Approach | NLL |
|---|---|
| `optim()` from the given start | `r round(ch_first$value, 2)` (threshold below zero) |
| 20 random starts | best `r round(min(ch_ms), 2)`; `r sum(ch_ms > ch_best$value + 1)` stuck on a plateau |
| **bounds**: `L-BFGS-B`, $t$ from 0 to 0.48 | **`r round(ch_lbfgsb$value, 2)`** |
| **grid over $t$**, then polish | **`r round(ch_best$value, 2)`** |

::: {.notes}
The figure is the whole story. The dotted lines are the least and most developed
routes. Left of zero, every route is past the threshold, so t stops mattering:
that is the plain development model, a plateau. Right of the most developed
route, no route is past it, so the development effect vanishes: a second, higher
plateau. The real answer is a narrow dip near zero, between them.

The default start, t = 0.3, sits on the slope down to the left plateau, and both
Nelder-Mead and BFGS slide straight off the data onto it. Random starts land on
either plateau about half the time.

What works is anything that keeps t inside the data: bounds (one argument), a
grid over the threshold with the other three parameters fitted at each value
(today's brute force, on one parameter), or annealing then polishing. Whoever
used one of those deserves the board.
:::

## What the best fit says {.smaller}

- Best threshold: **`r round(100 * ch_best$par[3], 1)`%** developed. Effectively
  **no safe level**: counts fall from the first few percent
- The threshold model beats the plain development model by
  **`r round(ch_first$value - ch_best$value, 1)`** NLL units, for one extra
  parameter: AIC prefers it by `r round(2 * (ch_first$value - ch_best$value) - 2, 1)`

::: {.plain}
The fitting problem and the biology agree: there is a threshold, and it is so close to zero that it barely matters.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two callbacks. The number of NLL units against one parameter is Lecture 18's
question; the AIC difference is 2 times the gain minus 2 for the extra
parameter, so the threshold earns its place, narrowly.

And the biology is a useful answer for a manager: there is no level of
development below which bobwhite are safe. The decline starts with the first
houses.

As ever with these counts, there are no zeros in the file, so this is the effect
of development on how many birds a route has given that it has any.
:::
